summary:
A trans visitor to Montana stands under the United States national travel-document regime. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth; new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. Travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports. A visitor's documents may therefore mismatch presentation or identity.

Entry carries a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Montana has enacted state restrictions that would ordinarily rank it among the country's worst jurisdictions, including a facility-use ban and a public-buildings bathroom ban, but Montana's courts have repeatedly blocked or enjoined those laws under the state constitution. Adult restrictions that were passed have not taken full effect. The practical position a visitor encounters in Montana therefore differs sharply from what the statutory book alone would suggest.

That court record makes Montana the single exception in the 2026 anti-trans legal-risk assessments: the only state whose grade improved, moving from 'worst laws' to 'high risk' in the February 2026 cycle as injunctions accumulated. The July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment ranks states by expert reading of bills covering adult and youth restrictions, and the same pattern of judicial blocking lifts Montana's standing in that assessment as well.
tangentialFactors:
Facility use is regulated in a substantial number of states, which matters for a visitor crossing state lines. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity; in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement is documented: in April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol and was arrested and handcuffed, which civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Identity documents remain the fastest-moving area of restriction across states. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers; rights groups describe the Kansas statute as a template other legislatures are following, with further targeting bills pending.

Foreign governments have responded publicly to the federal document and data rules. Multiple countries issued advisories warning trans citizens about travelling to the United States; at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

The national picture continues to tighten. A legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends. The youth-side picture remains unstable nationally, with federal policy shifts and litigation in flux.
localsOnly:
Montana residents who had hoped to use the state's statutory restrictions find that the courts have blocked or enjoined them under the state constitution, so adult restrictions passed by the legislature have not taken full effect. Litigation, not the text of the statutes, governs what is currently operative.

Identity-document rules for residents depend heavily on the state involved. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out, state by state, which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions, so the rules a resident encounters in Montana and in neighbouring states differ and must be checked against the current map.

The youth-side picture for residents is unsettled, with federal policy shifts and litigation driving changes that affect school-age restrictions as well as adult ones.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not identify which specific Montana statutes are currently enjoined, which remain in litigation, or when those cases are next heard; the standing of each measure is unresolved in this record.

No source in the inventory states whether Montana itself carries a do-not-travel designation in the 13 July 2026 assessment; only Idaho's designation and the national total of four are sourced. Montana's placement on any such list is therefore not stated here.

The outcome of the ACLU's lawsuit against the State Department, and the scope of any relief ultimately granted, are unresolved in the inventory beyond the Supreme Court's permission for the Department to proceed.

Whether Montana permits gender-marker changes on licences or birth certificates is not sourced in this inventory; readers are directed to the Movement Advancement Project map rather than to a claim about Montana specifically.
